Title: Understanding digital technology adoption in Javanese language teaching: A UTAUT-TPACK approach
Snippet: Path analysis of the structural model revealed TPACK competence and behavioral intention (BI) as predictors of the use of digital teaching behavior (DTB) in Javanese language teaching. The path coefficient from BI to DTB was β = 0.333 (p < 0.001), whereas that from TPACK to DTB was β = 0.485 (p < 0.001) (see Table 4). In addition, TPACK indirectly impacts DTB through BI, with an overall effect of 0.654. This finding indicates that TPACK competencies have direct effects on digital-based teaching behaviors and support behavioral intentions that, in turn, impact actual practice. This is in line with the theory of UTAUT2 by Venkatesh et al. (2012), which states that behavioral intention is a determining factor of behavior in the use of technology. In education, the correlation between the intention and behavior of technology use by teachers is also corroborated by previous research (Al-adwan et al., 2024;Hong et al., 2021), which suggests that teachers with a high intention to use technology have a greater frequency of use in classroom learning. Additionally, research conducted by Nguyen et al. (2020) showed that learning blog satisfaction among students had a positive effect on students' learning perceptions, which in turn had an effect on the intention and behavior of teachers toward the application of technology. 

TPACK competence, as a direct measure of DTB, provides insight into the fact that teachers with integrative technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge are better suited to integrate technology as part of their standard pedagogical routine. In their systematic reviews (Azhar & Hashim, 2022;Paidican & Arredondo, 2022), they emphasized the importance of TPACK building in teacher education to maximize effective technology integration in the classroom. Koh et al. (2014) noted that those with high TPACK scores are most likely to exhibit more habitual and innovative technology use behavior. Additionally, research conducted by Insani et al. (2024b) prioritized the role of local wisdom-based digital literacy in learning the local language, which can be utilized in Javanese language teaching.
</snippet>

Title: Technology Integration in Luna Central School: Challenges and Opportunities
Snippet: The data gathered from teacher-respondents at Luna Central School reveal that significant challenges continue to impede the effective integration of technology in classroom instruction. With an overall weighted mean of 3.7, teachers generally agree that these obstacles are substantial and persistent. Among the most pressing issues are technical barriers, as evidenced by a strong consensus regarding frequent technical issues and the lack of adequate technical support having a mean of 4.1. Unstable or slow internet connectivity indicated a mean of 3.7, further compounds these infrastructural deficiencies, making it difficult for teachers to consistently utilize digital tools and resources. Another critical challenge identified is the lack of sufficient training or professional development in the use of educational technology. Teachers agree as reflected in the mean of 4.0 that more targeted and ongoing training is necessary to build their confidence and competence in integrating technology effectively into their teaching practices. Additionally, while the limited availability of technological devices in classrooms received a moderate level of agreement with a mean of 3.5, it nonetheless represents a logistical hurdle that restricts the full realization of technology's potential in education. Time management also emerges as a concern, though to a lesser extent. Teachers only slightly agree as manifested by the mean of 3.2 that the use of technology disrupts class time, suggesting that while some difficulties exist, many educators have developed adaptive strategies to manage their lessons effectively, even when incorporating digital tools. Overall, these findings highlight that infrastructural limitations and insufficient training are the most critical barriers to successful technology integration at Luna Central School. Despite these challenges, teachers demonstrate a notable degree of resilience and adaptability, striving to incorporate technology into their teaching as effectively as possible, albeit under less-than-ideal circumstances. This underscores the need for systemic improvements in both infrastructure and professional development to bridge the gap between the intent to integrate technology and its practical execution in the classroom.
</snippet>

Title: The Relationship between Teacher Digital Literacy and the Use of Technology in Learning
Snippet: The findings will provide empirical evidence on how enhancing teachers' digital skills can lead to more effective technology integration in teaching, which, in turn, can improve student engagement, learning outcomes, and overall educational experiences. This research will also inform future policies aimed at supporting teachers' digital professional development, ensuring that educators are well-equipped to navigate the rapidly evolving digital landscape in education. 

While there is considerable literature on the importance of digital literacy for teachers, much of the existing research focuses on its general significance or the challenges faced by teachers in integrating technology into their teaching (Nacaroğlu & Göktaş, 2025;Quan & Baharom, 2025). Few studies have examined the specific relationship between teachers' digital literacy levels and the actual use of technology in the classroom. Moreover, much of the existing research is qualitative, focusing on individual case studies or small sample sizes, which limits the generalizability of findings. This study fills this gap by using a large sample size and quantitative methods to examine how different levels of digital literacy influence technology adoption in teaching. By focusing specifically on the correlation between digital literacy and technology use in the classroom, this research provides a more focused and comprehensive understanding of the issue. 

Additionally, many studies have explored the barriers to technology integration, such as access to resources or institutional support, but have not investigated how teachers' individual competencies, particularly in terms of digital literacy, influence their ability to overcome these barriers. This study expands on existing research by directly addressing the role of digital literacy in overcoming technological challenges faced by teachers (Sapkota, 2025;Yang dkk., 2025). The findings will contribute to the literature by providing a clearer picture of the factors that influence technology integration in education and offering evidence on the importance of teachers' digital skills in this process. 

The gap in the literature regarding the specific relationship between digital literacy and technology use in the classroom highlights the need for more empirical studies on this topic (Baymetov dkk., 2025;Sapkota, 2025). As educational systems increasingly focus on technologydriven teaching practices, understanding how teachers' digital literacy levels affect their use of technology is crucial for informing teacher training programs, curriculum development, and policy decisions. This study addresses this gap by providing empirical evidence on the direct link between teachers' digital skills and their ability to effectively integrate technology into their teaching practices.
</snippet>

Title: Rethinking Teacher Professional Development for the Digital Era: A Narrative Review
Snippet: These technologies not only augment instructional delivery but also reshape teacherstudent interactions and content engagement (Rubi & Sharma, 2024;Topalska, 2024). Incorporating such innovations into professional development requires adaptive, collaborative training models that build both technical proficiency and pedagogical confidence (Čakāne, 2025). Without such comprehensive support, teachers risk underutilizing these technologies, thereby limiting their potential to transform educational experiences. Global and regional statistics converge on the conclusion that addressing deficits in digital competence among teachers is an urgent educational priority. Sustainable, systematic, and ongoing professional development has been widely recognized as a cornerstone for preparing educators to meet the demands of twenty-first-century classrooms (Yadav, 2024;Setiawan, 2024). Yet, significant challenges persist. Chief among these is the insufficient digital competence among a large proportion of educators, which directly impedes the effective application of digital tools in instructional practice (Althubyani, 2024). Compounding this problem are structural issues such as heavy workloads and insufficient time, which prevent teachers from engaging in skill development alongside their instructional responsibilities (Morska et al., 2022). 

In addition to these barriers, uncertainty surrounding digital pedagogy remains a formidable challenge. Teachers are often tasked not only with learning how to operate digital tools but also with mastering the art of integrating them in ways that support interactive and engaging learning environments (Torres et al., 2020). Effective digital pedagogy requires adaptation of traditional instructional strategies to align with technology-enhanced modalities. Empirical evidence demonstrates that participation in professional training and collaborative communities of practice enhances teachers' capacity to integrate digital tools effectively (Portillo et al., 2020;Thannimalai & Raman, 2018). However, access to such professional opportunities is inconsistent, particularly in underserved rural areas where teachers face additional barriers to technological adoption (Nhung et al., 2025;Li, 2024). 

Despite considerable attention to digital competencies, notable gaps in the literature persist. While several studies have attempted to measure teachers' digital proficiency, relatively few have examined the long-term impact of professional development programs on classroom practices and student outcomes (Ma et al., 2025).
</snippet>

Snippet: Mooij and Smeets (2001) further state that if teachers do not trust their skills or competences to handle computers, they may be reluctant to introduce technology into their classroom. In other words, the integration of technology and teaching depends on the teacher's competence to master and use technology, and whether the teacher consciously uses technology to meet the teaching purpose. Therefore, this study sought to use online teaching as a mediation variable to investigate the impact of teachers' digital competence on online teaching behavior. Finally, teachers' digital competence is related to the characteristics of the situation in which they are placed. Porras-Hernández and Salinas-Amescua, 2013 consider that the characteristics of students (e.g., digital competence, learning motivation, knowledge of student thinking and learning) have an impact on teaching behavior. At the same time, knowledge of student characteristics is fundamental to teaching (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Considering the differences in students' digital abilities, it is inferred that students' digital competence will affect the role of teachers' digital competence. Therefore, this study selected the students' online learning difficulties perceived by teachers as the moderating variable, which could moderate the association between teachers' digital competence and the intention to use online teaching.

Title: Looking Into the Digital Age Teaching of Elementary Teachers in Kapalong District: A Mixed Method Study
Snippet: In the digital age, education and teaching management is facing many challenges and opportunities. Education and teaching management in the digital age lies in the struggle to adapt to rapid technological changes. Teachers and students face challenges such as limited digital skills, information security risks, and unequal access to technology, which contribute to the digital divide. At the same time, managing online learning environments and ensuring consistent education quality have become more complex. These issues demand targeted solutions like better teacher training, stronger infrastructure, and inclusive policies to ensure education remains effective and equitable (Tang et al., 2024). 

In the global context, particularly in Indonesia, it was found that teachers are facing a challenge such as lack of competence, deficient teaching materials, and inadequate digital teaching skills when integrating technology into their classrooms. It was found that limitation of infrastructures, such as low internet bandwidth and a scarcity of devices available in their schools. Teachers faced difficulties including the fact that they were not as familiar with technology as their students and had to learn new skills independently. One of the biggest challenges they faced was their own digital capabilities, and they recognized that they need to improve their skills to be able to effectively teach their students using technologies (Wahdidni et al., 2023). 

In the Philippines, specifically in the Quezon City, teachers have faced persistent challenges in integrating technology tools into teaching and learning. The primary barriers include a lack of competence in using ICT tools, which is closely followed by low confidence levels and resistance to change among educators. These factors significantly hinder the effective utilization of technology in classrooms. Time constraints within the instructional schedule and the limited application of technological resources further exacerbate these issues, making teaching more difficult. This situation reflects a broader trend observed in other parts of the Philippines. Many teachers across the country are inadequately trained in ICT, resulting in underutilization of digital tool (Buabeng-Andoh, 2020). 

Additionally, in the literature reviews included in this study, there are related studies on the present study such as the study of Jannah et al. (2020) entitled, <Elementary School Teachers' Perception of Digital Technology Based Learning in the 21st Century: Promoting Digital Technology as the Proponent Learning Tools= which discussed the impact of digital integration on the students' progress.

Title: Exploring Informatizaon Instructional Core Competence of Higher Vocational College Teacher for Professional Development
Snippet: Having analysed first-year teacher education students' comprehensive technology lesson plans, Valtonen et al. (2020) suggested that instructional knowledge plays the most crucial role in developing pre-service teachers' digital teaching competence (Seufert et al., 2021). This notion underscores the significance of instructional knowledge in the TPACK framework. Instructional knowledge competence indicators can comprehensively reflect teachers' teaching competence and level beyond the mere application and operation of technology (Bond et al., 2020). In digital teaching, teachers need to master the flexible use of various technological tools, integrating them with instructional content to enhance students' learning outcomes (Pinto & Leite, 2020). However, solely relying on technological competence and ignoring the absence of sufficient instructional knowledge may lead to issues such as the improper use of technology and suboptimal teaching (Taghizadeh & Hasani Yourdshahi, 2020). Therefore, competence indicators should promote the holistic development of teachers' digital teaching competence by including both technological and instructional knowledge. Additionally, these indicators should be tailored for different subjects and levels of teachers to more precisely enhance their capabilities and proficiency, providing effective guidance and support for their professional development (Basantes-Andrade et al., 2022). 

Technological knowledge competence indicators encompass self-management, as proposed by the UNESCO teachers' ICT competency framework (UNESCO, 2011), professional growth from the ISTE standards for educators (Whiting, 2017), teaching and learning based on the European framework for the digital competence of educators (EU Science Hub, 2017), and teaching methods from the UK's digital teaching framework (Education and Training Foundation, 2019). These indicators are associated with information technology skills related to teaching methods, the use of computer operation skills in teaching, and of information technology skills in organising and managing online courses (Chi et al., 2020). Among them, self-management, teaching and learning, teaching methods, and information technology skills related to teaching methods can be classified under classroom teaching, together with the use of computer operation skills in teaching, and of information technology skills in organising and managing online courses. In summary, classroom teaching and professional growth are both indicators of instructional knowledge competence.
</snippet>

Title: Assessment of class participation in online and offline learning environments: a qualitative investigation of teachers’ best practices and challenges
Snippet: This study addressed a gap by gathering current practices and challenges of teachers in assessing participation in both offline and online learning environments. Through the lens of outcome-based education (Biggs & Tang, 2011), we extended the knowledge base by identifying factors that drive the choice of assessment strategies and approaches, and by presenting potential solutions to long-standing issues in the practice of class participation assessment. 

First, the research highlights teachers' need for more professional development opportunities in the form of courses and hands-on training, that will help them improve current assessment practices. Institutions are highly encouraged to invest more in helping faculty develop materials for teaching with technology since technological tools appeared to be of help in managing their workload. Second, the provision of more support to teachers through teaching assistants and technical support could also help, as well as consistent sharing of experiences among teachers about updates in their classroom assessment practices. This could especially help novice teachers who are still navigating their way to teaching effectively. Third, teachers' acknowledgement of the value that technology-enabled assessment brings opens up opportunities for more inclusive participation assessment strategies, with students having more options to participate. Likewise, technology expands teachers' toolbox for assessment tasks, including class participation assessment. Thus, both researchers and practitioners must continuously review the functions and capacities of existing educational technologies to maximize their use in aiding teachers in assessing various forms of participation discussed in this article. Lastly, teachers must be able to set up an environment that encourages participation, since they consider students' feedback-seeking and students' use of that feedback to improve their work as participation. Ultimately, assessing participation communicates to students that teachers value their learning, and that what students say and what they do in class matters.
</snippet>

Title: Teachers’ Technological Competence of Pedagogical Strategies: Their Influence to Learners’ Performance
Snippet: In today's classrooms, integrating technology has become essential for enhancing teaching effectiveness and improving student learning outcomes. Teachers' technological competence-their ability to skillfully use digital tools and resources within pedagogical strategies-is a key factor in creating engaging and meaningful learning experiences (Tondeur, van Braak, Ertmer, & Ottenbreit-Leftwich, 2017). When used effectively, technology allows educators to design interactive lessons, provide differentiated instruction, and address the diverse needs of learners (Ertmer & Ottenbreit-Leftwich, 2010). 

Research indicates that teachers who are confident and competent in using technology are better equipped to implement innovative teaching methods, such as multimedia presentations, online assessments, and collaborative digital activities, which can significantly enhance student performance (Hsu, 2016). Technological competence also enables teachers to provide timely feedback, monitor student progress, and encourage self-directed learning, all of which contribute to higher engagement and achievement (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). 

Despite its importance, many teachers still encounter challenges in effectively integrating technology due to limited training, inadequate resources, or lack of confidence in using digital tools (Tondeur et al., 2017). In the context of Antique, exploring how teachers' technological competence influences their pedagogical strategies and learners' academic performance is crucial for improving instructional practices and learning outcomes. 

This study focuses on understanding the relationship between teachers' technological competence and learners' performance among 365 respondents in Antique during the 2024-2025 school year. Specifically, it examines teachers' skills in using digital tools, multimedia resources, online collaboration platforms, and assessment technologies, alongside learners' performance in terms of grades, task completion, and classroom participation. The study also investigates whether there is a significant relationship between teachers' technological competence and student outcomes, as well as whether factors such as age, gender, teaching experience, or grade level influence learners' performance. 

By addressing these questions, the study aims to provide practical insights into how technology can be effectively integrated into teaching to improve learning outcomes. The findings are intended to guide educators, school leaders, and policymakers in designing professional development programs and instructional interventions that harness technological tools to enhance teaching effectiveness and student achievement.
</snippet>

Title: Utilization of Digital Technology in Enhancing Teachers' Pedagogical Competence
Snippet: The use of digital technology has proven to have a positive impact on improving teachers' pedagogical competence. Based on interviews, many teachers feel that technology helps them develop more innovative and engaging teaching methods for students. With various digital platforms such as Google Classroom, Canva, and Quizizz, teachers can design more interactive lessons and provide a more enjoyable learning experience for students. Technology also allows teachers to diversify their teaching methods, such as utilizing educational videos, digital simulations, and interactive quizzes that enhance student engagement in the learning process. 

The use of digital technology boosts teachers' confidence in adopting technology-based teaching strategies and adapting their approaches according to students' needs. Technology enables them to adjust the pace and learning styles of each student, making learning more personalized and effective. It also allows teachers to use data and analysis of student learning outcomes to refine their teaching strategies. For example, with the analytics features available on digital learning platforms, teachers can track student progress more comprehensively and provide more specific feedback tailored to their individual needs (Habibulloh dkk., 2024). 

Observations conducted during the study also show that the use of digital technology has improved teacher-student interactions. In classrooms that incorporate technology-based learning, students are more active in asking questions and participating in discussions. Technology facilitates more dynamic two-way communication, such as through online discussion features in Google Classroom or interactive forums on other digital learning platforms. Teachers also have greater flexibility in delivering materials in various formats, such as interactive presentations, digital infographics, or simulations that enhance students' understanding of abstract concepts. This demonstrates that technology integration can improve teachers' communication skills and classroom management, which are essential aspects of pedagogical competence(Syafi'i & El-Yunusi, 2024). 

The use of digital technology in learning assists teachers in evaluation and assessment. With various online assessment tools such as Google Forms, Kahoot, and Microsoft Forms, teachers can develop a more objective and efficient grading system. Additionally, technology-based assessments enable teachers to provide faster and more detailed feedback to students. This not only enhances learning quality but also helps students understand their mistakes and correct them more quickly. Despite these benefits, there are still challenges in implementing digital technology to enhance teachers' pedagogical competence.
</snippet>

Title: The Relationship Between Teachers’ Perceived Classroom Management Abilities and Their Professional Digital Competence
Snippet: In recent decades, several researchers and academics have addressed issues relating to educational use of computers and other technologies. Both theoretical and empirical contributions have revolved around the influences that such tools could (or should) have on students' social, moral and academic learning outcomes. Important contributions on the concepts of computer literacy, media literacy, digital literacy and digital competence have been made since the 1990s. The teacher's role as a facilitator who must contextualize the use of ICT tools is strongly emphasized in the ICT field, which implicitly connects digital competence to classroom management. However, there is general agreement that the effective use of technology in teaching and learning practices is aligned with the general paradigm shift towards socio-cultural constructivist behavior and student-centered methods (Säljö 1999). Teachers who fear loss of control may experience such a paradigm shift as destabilizing and threatening (Bolick & Bartels 2015, Hickey & Schafer 2006, Brophy 2006); taking the perspective of dialectical pluralism and rejecting an either-or perspective, one can be informed by both of these paradigms. In both pre-service and in-service teacher training, there seems to be a general lack of awareness of the dynamics, vitality and diversity of classroom management (Evertson & Weinstein 2006). The concept of classroom management seems to be out of fashion, and academics and researchers tend to prefer phrases that elucidate the aims of classroom management rather than its techniques (Wubbels 2011). Standardized and internalized classroom management understandings are thus often adapted to a teacher-centered practice, associated with behavior management and sets of rules. However, the introduction of ICT tools in teaching and learning activities challenges the premises on which institutionalized solutions to behavioral issues are built. Ultimately it even challenges what really constitutes concepts such as classroom environment, learning, inclusion, relationships and behavioral issues as technologies offer additional (digital) venues and thus possibilities and limitations for managing teaching and learning activities. It would be interesting to further explore what might happen when a layer of ICT complexity is added to a static "crime-control" pre-understanding of classroom management. 

Several different positions and studies, dealing with digital competence and ICT in teaching and learning, share the assumption that teachers' professional digital competence is more complex than digital competence in other occupations and among average citizens.
</snippet>
<snippet id=23db93f4-6>
Title: The Digital Pedagogy Competence Scale (DiPeCoS): development and validation
Snippet: Many tools have been developed to evaluate a teacher's digital competence (see Table 1). A teacher's digital pedagogy competence is a subset of the teacher's digital competence and focuses on the purposeful use of digital technology for teaching and learning. 

According to the DigCompEdu Framework, teacher digital competence encompasses skilful application of technology in five areas. Besides teaching and learning, these areas include professional development, digital resources, assessment and feedback, and empowering learners (Redecker, 2017). Existing tools to evaluate a teacher's digital competence assess pedagogical skills, the application of technology in a range of classroom work, the educational institution and the community in the context of their own personal and professional development (Lázaro-Cantabrana et al., 2019). A literature review of existing tools 1 finds that most tools measure a teacher's digital competence, a concept that goes beyond digital pedagogy competence, and only a few tools focus on evaluating a teacher's digital pedagogy competence. 

Two tools that are closely related to the concept of teachers' digital pedagogy competence are the Survey of Preservice Teachers' Knowledge of Teaching and Technology (SPTKTT) by Schmidt et al. (2009), which is based on the TPACK model (Mishra & Koehler, 2006), and the UDL self-assessment tool by the University of Waikato (2018), based on the UDL framework (CAST, 2015). Both tools use Likert scale-based items to encourage teachers to reflect on their pedagogical practices (e.g., 'I know how to select effective teaching approaches to guide student thinking and learning in mathematics' on the SPTKTT and 'I encourage students to express their learning in multiple ways (e.g., essay, or video blog, poster or presentation)' on the UDL tool. Both tools rely on self-reports of respondents' behaviours, beliefs, perceptions, attitudes or intentions, which are shown to be virtually uncorrelated with their on-the-job behaviour (Thalheimer, 2018). Responding on selfreport scales is also often affected by social desirability bias (Van de Mortel, 2008), which can corrupt collected data.
</snippet>

Title: Promoting Primary School Chinese Teachers Teaching Competence
Snippet: Digitalization undoubtedly poses a significant challenge for teachers, prompting global attention on how they can effectively teach in this context to improve educational quality. The digital transformation of education involves digitizing the entire educational ecosystem, including the teaching environment, resources, and mindset. It extends beyond merely digitizing content or applying technology superficially. Teachers need to effectively and creatively use digital tools to reshape content, transform teaching models, innovate methods, and make informed decisions. This approach aims to foster student initiative, personalize guidance, improve educational outcomes, and support holistic student development (Huang & Du, 2021). Krumsvik (2011) argues that, within the digitalization landscape, teaching competence encompasses a teacher's ability to proficiently use information technology (IT) in education, their understanding of how IT influences pedagogical approaches, and their awareness of students' digital development. Furthermore, he emphasizes the importance of effectively integrating IT into teachers' classroom practices. Zheng (2019) tailored the components of teaching competence for digital education, identifying seven key areas: design and planning, development and implementation, teaching and assessment, management, pedagogical research, and attitudes towards the environment, health, and safety. While researchers may have varying interpretations of teaching competence in the digital era, there is a consensus on the importance of effectively integrating IT into teaching practices. The capability to integrate IT with teaching is considered a crucial aspect of teachers' teaching competence. However, it is also essential to emphasize changes in teachers' awareness and values in teaching and learning, rather than solely focusing on enhancing this ability (Caena & Redecker, 2019).
</snippet>

Title: Digital Competence of Teachers and Its Impact on Technology-Enhanced Teaching at Secondary Level
Snippet: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed educational systems worldwide, making digital competence an indispensable requirement for teachers at every educational level. The integration of technology into classroom instruction has shifted from being an optional pedagogical innovation to an essential component of effective teaching and learning. Governments, educational institutions, and policymakers have increasingly emphasized the importance of equipping teachers with the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to utilize digital technologies effectively for instructional purposes. Particularly at the secondary school level, where students require interactive, collaborative, and learner-centered educational experiences, teachers' digital competence plays a decisive role in determining the quality of technology-enhanced teaching. The effective use of digital technologies not only enriches classroom instruction but also promotes critical thinking, creativity, communication, and problemsolving skills among learners, which are considered essential competencies for the twenty-first century (Redecker, 2017;UNESCO, 2018;Falloon, 2020). Digital competence extends beyond the basic ability to operate computers or use educational software. It encompasses a comprehensive set of knowledge, technical skills, pedagogical abilities, ethical awareness, information literacy, communication capabilities, digital content creation, online collaboration, cybersecurity awareness, and continuous professional learning. Modern educational frameworks define digital competence as the confident, critical, responsible, and creative use of digital technologies for teaching, assessment, communication, collaboration, and lifelong learning. Teachers who possess high levels of digital competence are more likely to design innovative instructional activities, facilitate active learning environments, personalize instruction according to students' needs, and effectively integrate digital resources into curriculum delivery (Redecker, 2017;Ghomi & Redecker, 2019;Cabero-Almenara et al., 2021). The emergence of technology-enhanced teaching has significantly changed traditional pedagogical practices by integrating various digital tools such as learning management systems, virtual classrooms, multimedia presentations, online assessment platforms, educational applications, artificial intelligence, virtual laboratories, and collaborative digital environments into classroom instruction. Technology-enhanced teaching focuses not merely on using technological devices but on transforming teaching methodologies to improve learning outcomes, student engagement, knowledge construction, and instructional effectiveness.
</snippet>

Title: Digital empowerment for innovative teaching: application and mediating effects of information technology in physical education teachers’ practices
Snippet: The results of the mediation analysis indicate that teaching methods and content play a crucial role in bridging the relationship between IT teaching and assessment and management in innovative teaching, thereby supporting hypothesis 3 (Teaching methods and content mediate the relationship between IT teaching and assessment/management). This complete mediation effect (indirect effect = 0.519, direct effect = 0.005, n.s.) reveals a critical insight: technology's impact on innovative assessment practices is entirely contingent upon its integration with pedagogical methods. This finding problematizes simplistic "technology integration" approaches that focus on tool adoption without corresponding pedagogical transformation. The absence of a direct effect suggests that merely providing teachers with technology access-a common policy approach-is insufficient for improving assessment and management practices. Instead, the mediating mechanism underscores the primacy of pedagogical knowledge in determining whether and how technology enhances teaching innovation, supporting the TPACK framework's emphasis on the intersection rather than addition of technological and pedagogical knowledge. This finding supports Fullan's (2013) Stratosphere framework, which emphasizes that pedagogy must inform technology use rather than technology driving instruction. The mediating role of teaching methods confirms that effective technology integration requires deliberate pedagogical strategies to transform tools into meaningful teaching outcomes (62). It reveals that the use of document software can indirectly enhance teachers' performance in assessment and management by first improving their teaching methods and content. The explanation for this result may be that teachers can use documentation software to create richer teaching materials (such as course Outlines, sample questions, workbooks) and adjust lesson plans in real time based on student feedback (65). Optimized teaching content and methods can help students better understand knowledge points, and systematic teaching design can make classroom management more organized and reduce students' confusion and uncertainty. Moreover, multimedia software significantly influenced teaching methods and content, supporting its role in enhancing student engagement through dynamic and interactive instructional materials. Tools like video editing software allow PE teachers to visually demonstrate techniques and strategies, making lessons more accessible and engaging. Media equipment, though less influential than document software, contributes to innovative teaching by supporting interactive and collaborative activities in the classroom. Tools like smart boards and projectors enable teachers to present content effectively and facilitate real-time student participation.

I need to explain why teachers with high assessed digital competence underutilize technology. My plan is to synthesize evidence across: (a) the intention–behavior gap (UTAUT/TPB/TPACK), (b) classroom and curriculum constraints (time, assessment load), (c) infrastructure and platform issues, (d) professional development needs and skill specificity, and (e) self-report mismeasurement and beliefs/anxiety. I have already conducted four searches and found: (1) observational evidence that teachers with high perceived usefulness still show limited technical skills and infrastructure barriers; (2) UTAUT/TPB findings showing actual use depends on intention plus effort expectancy and facilitating conditions; (3) classroom-level barriers like limited time and rigid platforms; and (4) issues with self-report and alignment between assessment and teaching. To strengthen the case, I looked for evidence on student distraction/classroom management and interoperability/rigidity, but the retrieved snippets already cover many key factors. I will structure the answer around the main mechanisms: (1) intention vs. effort and support; (2) time/curriculum/assessment burdens; (3) infrastructure and platform rigidity; (4) skill specificity and PD gaps; (5) self-assessment mismeasurement and beliefs; and (6) student-centered pedagogy tensions and data/assessment needs. I will map claims to snippets: UTAUT/effort/facilitating (b591f485-3, b591f485-4, b591f485-8), time/PE barriers (b591f485-1), infrastructure/PD (b5430232-2, b5430232-4, 125fea59-4), specific skills/self-report mismatch (b5430232-2, b5430232-0), assessment/management and student distraction (b5430232-2, 23db93f4-5), and misalignment of purpose (b5430232-2, 23db93f4-6). I will acknowledge that high competence can still face constraints and that self-report may not match behavior. Now I will synthesize into a coherent answer with sections and citations.</think>

# Why teachers with high assessed digital competence still underutilize technology

## 1) Intention does not guarantee behavior: effort and support matter
Even when teachers intend to use technology, actual use depends on perceived effort and on having supportive conditions in place. UTAUT/UTAUT2 and related models consistently find that effort expectancy and facilitating conditions (training, support, resources) predict both intention and actual behavior; in several studies, effort expectancy can even inversely relate to intention among more digitally literate teachers because they focus more on value than ease, leaving a gap between intention and use if effort remains high or support is thin<cite id="b591f485-3">In education, the correlation between the intention and behavior of technology use by teachers is corroborated, with TPACK proficiency and facilitating conditions predicting actual use; effort expectancy can have a negative effect because more experienced teachers with higher digital literacy place less emphasis on ease of use.</cite><cite id="b591f485-4">A meta-analytic SEM across 44 studies confirms that performance and effort expectancies, social influence, and facilitating conditions shape teachers' behavior; facilitating conditions exert an indirect effect via intention, indicating that support conditions and perceived ease/usability must be addressed to translate intentions into use.</cite><cite id="b591f485-8">Applications of UTAUT in educational contexts show mixed results: facilitating conditions and performance expectancy often drive intention, but actual use can be curtailed by the absence of these conditions or by added constraints, revealing contradictions between intention and behavior when conditions are insufficient.</cite>.

## 2) Classroom time and curriculum alignment are binding constraints
Teachers report that limited class time, rigid curricula, and misalignment with standards constrain technology use, even when they are competent and willing. In physical education, teachers specifically note that short class durations and lack of dedicated training restrict integration; more generally, external barriers include limited time and insufficient expertise, while internal barriers reflect adherence to established practices<cite id="b591f485-1">External barriers impeding technology integration include limited time, insufficient expertise, and inadequate resources; internal barriers relate to teacher beliefs and adherence to established pedagogical practices.</cite>. Reviews emphasize that policy-expectation and classroom practice gaps persist because training, resources, and institutional support are inadequate, preventing meaningful integration despite competence<cite id="125fea59-1">A major challenge is the gap between policy and classroom implementation; inadequate training, limited resources, and insufficient institutional support hinder technology integration, constraining its effectiveness in practice.</cite>.

## 3) Infrastructure and platform rigidity limit usable integration
Persistent infrastructure gaps—slow/unstable connectivity, insufficient devices, and limited technical support—prevent reliable classroom use, which especially frustrates competent teachers who otherwise could integrate technology effectively<cite id="125fea59-4">Teachers identify frequent technical issues, lack of adequate technical support, and unstable/slow internet connectivity as critical barriers, with limited device availability and insufficient training further constraining integration.</cite>. Rigid platforms and complex systems also hinder adoption; teachers report that inflexible tools and limited interoperability impede their ability to use technology in ways that fit their pedagogy and workflow<cite id="b5430232-1">Rigid digital platforms act as barriers for educators, underscoring the need for adaptable, inclusive tools; structured training is necessary because self-directed learning alone is insufficient.</cite>.

## 4) Professional development needs are domain-specific and ongoing
High assessments of competence can miss domain-specific gaps that block classroom integration, such as spreadsheet/data analysis skills for assessment or advanced classroom management with digital tools. Observational evidence shows that teachers who self-report usefulness still struggle with advanced tools (e.g., spreadsheets) and rely on manual processes; they also note that informal learning is inadequate and structured mentoring is needed<cite id="b5430232-0">Observation corroborates interview claims of limited experience with productivity software; teachers need structured training with direct mentoring for advanced skills like formulas, validation, pivot tables, and charts.</cite>. Reviews highlight that workload and insufficient time further obstruct participation in PD and iterative skill-building, so even competent teachers underutilize technology when they cannot devote time to deepen practice<cite id="125fea59-6">Structural issues such as heavy workloads and insufficient time prevent teachers from engaging in skill development alongside instructional responsibilities, contributing to persistent barriers.</cite>.

## 5) Self-assessment mismeasurement and beliefs/anxiety can mislead
Self-report instruments often do not align with on-the-job behavior; teachers may overestimate competence or report confidence that does not translate into effective, habitual use. Reviews note that self-reports are "virtually uncorrelated with on-the-job behavior," and social desirability bias can inflate perceived competence, masking specific gaps that limit actual use<cite id="b5430232-2">Evidence highlights persistent digital inequities and generational divides, with internal barriers like beliefs and confidence shaping intentions more than external factors in some contexts; self-assessed competence may not reflect observed practice.</cite><cite id="b5430232-0">Interviews and observations reveal a mismatch between perceived usefulness/competence and actual ability to operate digital assessment systems, with teachers acknowledging specific technical gaps despite general confidence.</cite><cite id="b5430232-6">Studies report teachers' limited ability to integrate technology beyond sporadic use; shortcomings are often attributed to neglected digital competence and the need for further training, underscoring measurement challenges and gaps between desired and actual use.</cite><cite id="b5430232-6">Self-report measures have limitations, and teachers may exhibit a gap between desired and actual use due to inadequate training and support.</cite>.

## 6) Purpose–practice misalignment: technology for assessment vs. teaching, and classroom management concerns
Technology is often adopted for assessment and administrative tasks rather than for pedagogically transformative teaching, limiting underuse in the classroom. Teachers report that technology can disrupt class time, and they worry about managing student behavior and ensuring productive engagement with devices; these concerns are heightened when tools do not support clear instructional goals or when teachers fear loss of control<cite id="125fea59-4">Teachers note that technology use can disrupt class time, though infrastructural and training gaps are more critical; time management emerges as a secondary concern.</cite><cite id="23db93f4-5">Teachers' classroom management perspectives interact with technology adoption; fears of loss of control and a narrow, rule-focused view of management can impede technology integration, which challenges traditional behavioral premises.</cite>. Moreover, technology's role in assessment can divert attention from teaching practice, and without supportive environments and PD, competent teachers may default to low-risk uses that do not change pedagogy<cite id="b5430232-2">Structural inequities and internal barriers shape teachers' intentions and practices; changes in external conditions like vision and PD influence integration and evolving beliefs about classroom technology use.</cite>.

## 7) Synthesis: competence is necessary but not sufficient
Competence increases the possibility of effective integration, but actual classroom use depends on supportive conditions: time, infrastructure, flexible tools, and ongoing, domain-specific PD aligned to curriculum and assessment goals. When these conditions are absent, teachers with high assessed competence still underutilize technology because effort and constraints outweigh perceived usefulness, intentions stall without support, and specific pedagogical purposes are not met<cite id="b591f485-4">Facilitating conditions influence behavior indirectly via intention, so even competent teachers will underuse technology if support, ease, and relevance are lacking.</cite><cite id="125fea59-1">Inadequate training, resources, and institutional support hinder integration despite policy expectations, creating a persistent classroom practice gap.</cite><cite id="b5430232-0">Observed practice often lags behind perceived competence due to specific technical gaps and infrastructure constraints, indicating that competence alone does not ensure use.</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Digitalizing Multiple Intelligence Assessment in Early Childhood: A Needs Analysis from Teachers' Perspectives
Snippet: Despite high perceived usefulness, interview and observational data converged in revealing significant barriers related to perceived ease of use-teachers' confidence in their ability to successfully operate digital assessment systems. Analysis identified two primary barrier categories: limited digital competence among teachers and inadequate technological infrastructure at the institutional level. 

Limited digital literacy. Interview data revealed considerable variation in teachers' digital competence, with most participants describing their technology skills as basic and insufficient for advanced spreadsheet operation. A senior teacher with six years of experience articulated this limitation: "I have been teaching for 6 years, but my experience with technology is still limited. I can use WhatsApp and social media, but for more technical things like Excel or Google Sheets, I am still unfamiliar. Sometimes I feel left behind compared to younger teachers who are more tech-savvy." This statement illustrates both the specific skill gap (familiarity with communication apps but not productivity software) and the psychological dimension of technology anxiety, particularly in relation to generational differences in digital fluency. 

Teachers' self-reported competence limitations were validated through observation of their current technology use in classroom and administrative contexts. During the four-week observation period, teachers were observed using smartphones primarily for communication (WhatsApp groups for parent communication) and simple photography (documenting children's activities). No instances of teachers using computers for data management, analysis, or report generation were observed, with all documentation activities conducted through manual handwriting. This observational evidence corroborates interview claims of limited experience with productivity software and data management tools. 

Even among younger teachers who expressed greater comfort with technology generally, specific gaps in spreadsheet competency were evident. Teachers reported familiarity with basic data entry but acknowledged lacking skills in formula creation, data validation, pivot table use, or chart generation-precisely the functions that would be most valuable for assessment data analysis and reporting. A younger teacher explained: "I once tried to learn Excel on my own from YouTube, but it's also difficult to learn alone. Sometimes I don't know where to start, and if there's an error I don't know how to solve it. I need structured training with direct mentoring." This statement highlights not only skill deficits but also unsuccessful prior attempts at self-directed learning, suggesting that informal learning approaches may be insufficient and that structured professional development is necessary.

Title: Building a Training Model to Enhance Digital Competencies Among Learning Support Teachers in Jordan: Examining the Role of Gender, Academic Qualifications, and Teaching Experience
Snippet: The post-pandemic acceleration of digital education has also benefited early-career teachers, who entered the profession during a period of rapid technological integration [30]. As a result, they tend to display higher adaptability, greater openness to innovation, and more frequent use of digital platforms in both personal and professional contexts [24]. While this finding aligns with previous research highlighting younger teachers' relative advantage in digital skills, the study introduces a novel perspective by indicating that rigid digital platforms can act as barriers for certain educators, particularly those supporting students with diverse learning needs. This underscores that efforts to enhance digital competence should extend beyond training programs to include the design and implementation of flexible, adaptable digital tools that facilitate inclusive education. Together, these factors help explain observed competency gaps and emphasize the importance of differentiated, targeted professional development initiatives aimed at equipping more experienced teachers with up-to-date digital pedagogical skills, thereby enabling effective integration of technology in diverse classroom contexts. 

Recent studies indicate that teachers with less than ten years of experience often demonstrate higher levels of digital fluency than their more experienced counterparts [19,23]. This advantage stems not only from early and prolonged exposure to technology but also from comprehensive academic and professional training. In particular, graduate programs in Jordan integrate extensive coursework and research in educational technology, digital pedagogy, and instructional design. They provide graduates with the theoretical knowledge and practical skills necessary to effectively integrate digital learning. Those graduates develop advanced skills in critical thinking, analytical evaluation, and content synthesis, enabling them to design, adapt, and implement pedagogically robust digital learning modules. 

Teachers with advanced degrees tend to demonstrate greater competence in reflective practice, regularly evaluating and improving the effectiveness of digital tools to meet the needs of diverse learners, including those with special educational needs. Their participation in professional development activities (e.g., specialized conferences, workshops, and research networks) ensures they keep pace with emerging trends in educational technology [23]. Evidence from a systematic review suggests that younger teachers and those with postgraduate qualifications report higher self-assessed digital competence, while more experienced teachers often demonstrate moderate to low confidence in technology-enhanced assessment [27].

Title: Identifying Multilevel Predictors of Digipedagogical Competence among Secondary School Teachers in the United States
Snippet: While a significant body of research on digital competence exists, especially in European contexts (e.g., Guille´n-Ga´mez et al., 2021;Szabo´et al., 2022;L. Tomczyk et al., 2023), research within the U.S. educational context remains relatively limited in terms of largescale investigations that explore the systemic and institutional factors influencing digital teaching proficiency among secondary teachers. In the U.S., digital competence or skills is often framed within broader frameworks such as the International Society for Technology in Education (ISTE) Standards for Educators (ISTE, 2017), which emphasize educator roles such as facilitator, designer, and learner in integrating technology effectively. Although teachers may possess the skills to integrate technology into their teaching, they might still encounter barriers, such as inadequate equipment, intrinsic or extrinsic factors, and limitations within the school setting, that hinder their capability to do so effectively (Ertmer et al., 2012;Hathaway et al., 2024). Moreover, structural inequities tied to socioeconomic, geographic, and institutional factors contribute to what van Dijk (2006) describes as the second-level digital divide, which encompasses disparities not only in access but also in motivation, skills, and usage. In a study of teachers' technology practices within a low-SES U.S. school district, Makki et al. (2018) found that internal barriers, such as beliefs and confidence, played a greater role in shaping teachers' intentions to use technology than external factors. Recent findings also underscore the persistence of digital inequities and generational divides among U.S. secondary school teachers, further complicating efforts to advance equitable digital competence across schools (Avci et al., 2025). In a study involving in-service middle and high school teachers from 18 schools across the United States, Xie et al. (2023) found that changes in external conditions, such as technology integration vision and effective professional development, significantly influenced teachers' integration of digital resources and their evolving beliefs about technology use in classrooms.

Title: A qualitative comparison of competence frameworks for teacher educators’ digital competence
Snippet: Most of the research on digital competences has focused on students, in-service and pre-service teachers [18]. Karimi and Khawaja [19] also claim that there is significantly less material available regarding the digital competence of university than school-level teachers. 

In their literature review on strategies for preparing prospective teachers for the professional use of digital technologies, Tondeur, Trevisan, Howard, and van Braak [20] repeatedly found evidence that role models (meaning teacher educators) play a decisive role in this process. This conclusion aligns with the study by Momdjian, Manegre, and Gutiérrez-Colón [21], who investigated different approaches to develop pre-service teachers' digital competence in Lebanon, and report that teacher educators emerge as the key factor influencing pre-service teachers' overall digital competence development. Existing related work on teacher educators suggests that they may often face institutional barriers to integrate digital technologies successfully into teacher education, and may also often lack the competence to do so. Avidov Ungar and Forkosh Baruch [22] investigated facilitating and hindering factors for the ICT implementation in teacher education institutes in Israel. One of the hindering factors that they found was the lack of skills, knowledge and instruction. Amhag, Hellström, and Stigmar [23] investigated the use of digital tools of teacher educators at two Swedish universities and found that they do not use digital tools primarily for pedagogical purposes. Although most of the surveyed teacher educators self-evaluated their digital competence as better than low, the majority reported a need for more training in that field. This suggests that the gap between the desired and actual use of technology may partly be caused by a lack of adequate professional development programs. 

Reviews regarding the digital competence of university teachers more generally found that most studies indicate a low level of digital competence among university teachers, and a need for further training [24,25]. Karimi and Khawaja [19] conducted a systematic literature review to identify barriers that teachers in higher education face regarding their digital competence. 70% of the studies they analyzed mentioned a lack of training and professional development for higher education teachers as a barrier.

Title: Teachers’ professional digital competence: an overview of conceptualisations in the literature
Snippet: Studies in higher education research (Spante et al., 2018) have highlighted these shortcomings in relation to teacher students' preparedness for teaching with digital technology (e.g., Helleve et al., 2020;Howard et al., 2021;Lund & Aagaard, 2020), teacher educators' professional digital competence (e.g., Carpenter et al., 2020;Instefjord & Munthe, 2017;Krumsvik, 2011Krumsvik, , 2014;;Lund et al., 2014;Uerz et al., 2018) and in-service teachers' development of digital competence and attitudes towards technology (e.g., Björk Gudmundsdottir & Hatlevik, 2018;Pongsakdi et al., 2021;Starkey, 2020). One way to uncover and delineate what competences teachers need for teaching in digitalised classrooms has been to develop different frameworks, for example, the comprehensive DigCompEdu (European Commission, 2021), ICT competency framework for teachers (UNESCO, 2021) and TPACK. 1 The latter is developed by Mishra and Koehler (2006) and identifies the three following knowledge areas: 1) technological, 2) pedagogical and content and 3) the integration of these. As well as constituting a conceptual framework, TPACK has been used to empirically study how these knowledge areas are enacted in specific teaching contexts, which has contributed to understandings of the numerous factors that play into teachers' work in the classroom (e.g., Pareto & Willermark, 2019). Thus, a general tendency in educational research has been for studies to report on teachers' limited ability to integrate technologies into their teaching in a way that extends beyond the sporadic use of digital tools (e.g., Lund & Aagaard, 2020;Novella-García & Cloquell-Lozano, 2021;Sanders & George, 2017). 

Such shortcomings are often based on the critique that digital competence as content has been neglected in both teacher education and professional development efforts. Title: Bibliometric analysis and systematic review of digital competence in education
Snippet: The ubiquity of digital technologies has profoundly transformed communication and education in the 21st century, making the development of digital competence essential for both teachers and students to be prepared for the digital age. However, existing reviews predominantly focus on the teachers’ perspective with a limited scope and methodology. This literature review combines bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review to provide a comprehensive analysis of existing research. Bibliometric analysis evaluates performance and science mapping to identify influential journals, countries, and authors while visualizing trends in the field. Content analysis identifies five major themes: (1) digital competence levels, (2) factors and variables, (3) digital competence and teacher education, (4) students’ digital competence, and (5) digital competence and academic performance. The study also outlines seven future research directions: (1) integrating digital competence into curricula, (2) initial training in digital competence for future professions, (3) subject-specific development, (4) expanding research samples to include younger students, (5) addressing limitations of self-assessment, (6) understanding the needs of teachers and students, and (7) strengthening administrative support. Overall, the review highlights challenges in measuring digital competence and underscores the need for its integration into education systems, offering insights into opportunities for future research.

Title: Graduate Students' Competence in Online Work Employability
Snippet: This section explores the competencies in internet search and distance learning among teachers, which are increasingly crucial in the modern educational landscape. The findings suggest a mixed profile of digital readiness among teachers: while they are generally confident in core internet skills and basic distance learning tasks, they show weaknesses in more technical or specialized areas of online engagement. This pattern has been documented in research on digital competence in education. In a large-scale review of teachers' ICT competencies, researchers found that although basic and pedagogical uses of technology were relatively well developed, teachers were less confident when faced with technical troubleshooting, adapting technologies for complex tasks, or integrating high-level digital resources into instruction (Tondeur et al., 2017). 

The findings imply that while teachers demonstrate strong competencies in fundamental internet and distance learning skills, there are notable gaps in their ability to handle specific technical issues and access specialized online resources.

Title: Developing a digital competence scale for teachers: validity and reliability study
Snippet: Within the scope of updated education programs, teachers should have digital competence to use digital technologies more efficiently in the education process and improve students' digital skills (Instefjord & Munthe, 2017). Previous studies have shown that the digital experiences of teachers during their undergraduate education affect their ability to use their digital competence effectively and efficiently in their professional life (Tomte et al., 2015). Having digital skills is essential for teachers in terms of being aware of the development of technology and integrating these technologies into teaching (Hatlevik & Christophersen, 2013). Teachers' lack of these skills can negatively affect many aspects, from students' academic success to the general outcomes of the education system (Yazar & Keskin, 2016). Also, it is stated in previous studies that the deficiencies in the education system are due to the low levels of teacher digital competence (Hanell, 2018). Having high digital competencies of teachers will not only facilitate digital learning of students and increase their motivation, but also will improve their learning quality and support faster and more enjoyable learning (Caena & Redecker, 2019;Redecker, 2017). Therefore, as technology develops and new technologies are integrated into schools, teachers need to develop their digital skills accordingly (Starkey, 2020). There are many reports and frameworks that provide guidance for teachers to develop their digital competence (Carretero et al., 2017;ISTE, 2017;OECD, 2019;UNESCO, 2018). According to these reports and frameworks, teachers should have digital skills and constantly improve themselves in information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, Safety, problem-solving, and similar competencies. Also, it is considered that designing valid and reliable measurement tools that can determine the digital competencies of teachers and eliminate the deficiencies by revealing the digital profiles of teachers within the scope of these reports and frameworks will play a significant role in the development of teachers' digital competence.

As a result, they tend to display higher adaptability, greater openness to innovation, and more frequent use of digital platforms in both personal and professional contexts [24]. While this finding aligns with previous research highlighting younger teachers' relative advantage in digital skills, the study introduces a novel perspective by indicating that rigid digital platforms can act as barriers for certain educators, particularly those supporting students with diverse learning needs. This underscores that efforts to enhance digital competence should extend beyond training programs to include the design and implementation of flexible, adaptable digital tools that facilitate inclusive education. Together, these factors help explain observed competency gaps and emphasize the importance of differentiated, targeted professional development initiatives aimed at equipping more experienced teachers with up-to-date digital pedagogical skills, thereby enabling effective integration of technology in diverse classroom contexts. 

Recent studies indicate that teachers with less than ten years of experience often demonstrate higher levels of digital fluency than their more experienced counterparts [19,23]. This advantage stems not only from early and prolonged exposure to technology but also from comprehensive academic and professional training. In particular, graduate programs in Jordan integrate extensive coursework and research in educational technology, digital pedagogy, and instructional design. They provide graduates with the theoretical knowledge and practical skills necessary to effectively integrate digital learning. Those graduates develop advanced skills in critical thinking, analytical evaluation, and content synthesis, enabling them to design, adapt, and implement pedagogically robust digital learning modules.

snippet.text: The ubiquity of digital technologies has profoundly transformed communication and education in the 21st century, making the development of digital competence essential for both teachers and students to be prepared for the digital age. However, existing reviews predominantly focus on the teachers’ perspective with a limited scope and methodology. This literature review combines bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review to provide a comprehensive analysis of existing research. Bibliometric analysis evaluates performance and science mapping to identify influential journals, countries, and authors while visualizing trends in the field. Content analysis identifies five major themes: (1) digital competence levels, (2) factors and variables, (3) digital competence and teacher education, (4) students’ digital competence, and (5) digital competence and academic performance. The study also outlines seven future research directions: (1) integrating digital competence into curricula, (2) initial training in digital competence for future professions, (3) subject-specific development, (4) expanding research samples to include younger students, (5) addressing limitations of self-assessment, (6) understanding the needs of teachers and students, and (7) strengthening administrative support. Overall, the review highlights challenges in measuring digital competence and underscores the need for its integration into education systems, offering insights into opportunities for future research.

This section explores the competencies in internet search and distance learning among teachers, which are increasingly crucial in the modern educational landscape. The findings suggest a mixed profile of digital readiness among teachers: while they are generally confident in core internet skills and basic distance learning tasks, they show weaknesses in more technical or specialized areas of online engagement. This pattern has been documented in research on digital competence in education. In a large-scale review of teachers' ICT competencies, researchers found that although basic and pedagogical uses of technology were relatively well developed, teachers were less confident when faced with technical troubleshooting, adapting technologies for complex tasks, or integrating high-level digital resources into instruction (Tondeur et al., 2017). 

The findings imply that while teachers demonstrate strong competencies in fundamental internet and distance learning skills, there are notable gaps in their ability to handle specific technical issues and access specialized online resources.

snippet.text: Within the scope of updated education programs, teachers should have digital competence to use digital technologies more efficiently in the education process and improve students' digital skills (Instefjord & Munthe, 2017). Previous studies have shown that the digital experiences of teachers during their undergraduate education affect their ability to use their digital competence effectively and efficiently in their professional life (Tomte et al., 2015). Having digital skills is essential for teachers in terms of being aware of the development of technology and integrating these technologies into teaching (Hatlevik & Christophersen, 2013). Teachers' lack of these skills can negatively affect many aspects, from students' academic success to the general outcomes of the education system (Yazar & Keskin, 2016). Also, it is stated in previous studies that the deficiencies in the education system are due to the low levels of teacher digital competence (Hanell, 2018). Having high digital competencies of teachers will not only facilitate digital learning of students and increase their motivation, but also will improve their learning quality and support faster and more enjoyable learning (Caena & Redecker, 2019;Redecker, 2017). Therefore, as technology develops and new technologies are integrated into schools, teachers need to develop their digital skills accordingly (Starkey, 2020). There are many reports and frameworks that provide guidance for teachers to develop their digital competence (Carretero et al., 2017;ISTE, 2017;OECD, 2019;UNESCO, 2018). According to these reports and frameworks, teachers should have digital skills and constantly improve themselves in information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, Safety, problem-solving, and similar competencies. Also, it is considered that designing valid and reliable measurement tools that can determine the digital competencies of teachers and eliminate the deficiencies by revealing the digital profiles of teachers within the scope of these reports and frameworks will play a significant role in the development of teachers' digital competence.

documents.snippet:
Despite high perceived usefulness, interview and observational data converged in revealing significant barriers related to perceived ease of use-teachers' confidence in their ability to successfully operate digital assessment systems. Analysis identified two primary barrier categories: limited digital competence among teachers and inadequate technological infrastructure at the institutional level. 

Limited digital literacy. Interview data revealed considerable variation in teachers' digital competence, with most participants describing their technology skills as basic and insufficient for advanced spreadsheet operation. A senior teacher with six years of experience articulated this limitation: "I have been teaching for 6 years, but my experience with technology is still limited. I can use WhatsApp and social media, but for more technical things like Excel or Google Sheets, I am still unfamiliar. Sometimes I feel left behind compared to younger teachers who are more tech-savvy." This statement illustrates both the specific skill gap (familiarity with communication apps but not productivity software) and the psychological dimension of technology anxiety, particularly in relation to generational differences in digital fluency. 

Teachers' self-reported competence limitations were validated through observation of their current technology use in classroom and administrative contexts. During the four-week observation period, teachers were observed using smartphones primarily for communication (WhatsApp groups for parent communication) and simple photography (documenting children's activities). No instances of teachers using computers for data management, analysis, or report generation were observed, with all documentation activities conducted through manual handwriting. This observational evidence corroborates interview claims of limited experience with productivity software and data management tools. 

Even among younger teachers who expressed greater comfort with technology generally, specific gaps in spreadsheet competency were evident. Teachers reported familiarity with basic data entry but acknowledged lacking skills in formula creation, data validation, pivot table use, or chart generation-precisely the functions that would be most valuable for assessment data analysis and reporting. A younger teacher explained: "I once tried to learn Excel on my own from YouTube, but it's also difficult to learn alone. Sometimes I don't know where to start, and if there's an error I don't know how to solve it. I need structured training with direct mentoring." This statement highlights not only skill deficits but also unsuccessful prior attempts at self-directed learning, suggesting that informal learning approaches may be insufficient and that structured professional development is necessary.

In a large-scale review of teachers' ICT competencies, researchers found that although basic and pedagogical uses of technology were relatively well developed, teachers were less confident when faced with technical troubleshooting, adapting technologies for complex tasks, or integrating high-level digital resources into instruction (Tondeur et al., 2017). 

The findings imply that while teachers demonstrate strong competencies in fundamental internet and distance learning skills, there are notable gaps in their ability to handle specific technical issues and access specialized online resources.

documents.snippet: Within the scope of updated education programs, teachers should have digital competence to use digital technologies more efficiently in the education process and improve students' digital skills (Instefjord & Munthe, 2017). Previous studies have shown that the digital experiences of teachers during their undergraduate education affect their ability to use their digital competence effectively and efficiently in their professional life (Tomte et al., 2015). Having digital skills is essential for teachers in terms of being aware of the development of technology and integrating these technologies into teaching (Hatlevik & Christophersen, 2013). Teachers' lack of these skills can negatively affect many aspects, from students' academic success to the general outcomes of the education system (Yazar & Keskin, 2016). Also, it is stated in previous studies that the deficiencies in the education system are due to the low levels of teacher digital competence (Hanell, 2018). Having high digital competencies of teachers will not only facilitate digital learning of students and increase their motivation, but also will improve their learning quality and support faster and more enjoyable learning (Caena & Redecker, 2019;Redecker, 2017). Therefore, as technology develops and new technologies are integrated into schools, teachers need to develop their digital skills accordingly (Starkey, 2020). There are many reports and frameworks that provide guidance for teachers to develop their digital competence (Carretero et al., 2017;ISTE, 2017;OECD, 2019;UNESCO, 2018). According to these reports and frameworks, teachers should have digital skills and constantly improve themselves in information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, Safety, problem-solving, and similar competencies. Also, it is considered that designing valid and reliable measurement tools that can determine the digital competencies of teachers and eliminate the deficiencies by revealing the digital profiles of teachers within the scope of these reports and frameworks will play a significant role in the development of teachers' digital competence.

Title: Predicting the power of informal learning opportunities on technology use of physical education teachers
Snippet: The increasing prevalence and accessibility of digital technologies have prompted researchers to examine teachers' receptivity and utilisation of these tools in the classroom (17).
